uncited: Appearance Implicit Neural Representations define the mapping from spatial coordinates and viewing directions to the final color and opacity of a volume rendering ray.
This method solves the problem of how to encode view-dependent effects (such as specular highlights or subsurface scattering) and view-independent albedo within a neural field framework.
The core mechanism of Appearance Implicit Neural Representations is the evaluation of a color prediction network, denoted as $MLP$, which outputs the color $c_i$ for a sample point $p_i$ along a ray.
The input to this network consists of positional encodings $\gamma(p_i)$ and geometric or appearance features derived from the scene representation.
**Coupled (base)**: Color is jointly encoded with geometry using only the geometric encoding $\Phi^*(p_i)$ and positional encoding.
There are no additional channeled geometric features passed to the color network.
**Coupled**: Color is jointly encoded with geometry, but additionally receives channeled geometric features $h_i$.
These features $h_i$ are typically extracted from an intermediate layer of the geometric network $\Phi$ and passed explicitly to the color network.
**Decoupled**: Color is independently encoded by a separate appearance network $\phi^*$, distinct from the geometric network $\Phi$.
The geometric features $\Phi^*(p_i)$ are not used as input to the color network.
Uses a shared network or shared features for geometry and color.
Uses separate networks for geometry and appearance.

The distinction between coupled and decoupled appearance modeling has become a critical design choice in recent Neural Implicit Representation (INR) research, particularly in the context of RGB-D SLAM and real-time rendering.
Recent benchmarking work has highlighted that the choice of structure significantly affects the initialization phase of INRs trained on single posed RGB-D frames.
While coupled structures accelerate SDF convergence, they can hinder color accuracy in high-resolution dense representations.
